---
title: "occam's razor in ml"
---

## the principle

- among hypotheses that explain the data about equally well, prefer the simplest one
- originally a philosophical heuristic (attributed to william of ockham), adopted in ml as a practical guide for choosing between models that fit the training data comparably
- "simplest" in ml usually means fewest parameters, lowest-degree polynomial, shallowest tree, fewest nonzero coefficients, or smallest hypothesis class — not simplest to explain in words

## why simpler is favoured in ml

- **sample complexity**: in [pac learning](pac-learning.qmd#sample-complexity), the number of examples needed to generalise reliably grows with the complexity of the hypothesis class ($\ln\lvert\mathcal{h}\rvert$, or vc dimension for infinite classes) — a simpler class needs less data to guarantee low error at the same confidence level, which is a formal reason simpler models generalise better from limited data
- **minimum description length (mdl)**: formalises occam's razor information-theoretically — prefer the hypothesis $h$ minimising $l(h)+l(d\mid h)$, the number of bits to describe the hypothesis plus the number of bits to describe the data given that hypothesis; a model that fits the training data perfectly but takes many bits to describe (e.g. memorising every point) is penalised against a simpler model with slightly higher error

## information criteria: aic & bic

- the akaike information criterion directly trades off fit against complexity: $\text{aic}=2k-2\ln\hat l$, where $k$ is the number of fitted parameters and $\hat l$ is the model's maximised likelihood — lower aic is better
- the bayesian information criterion does the same with a heavier complexity penalty: $\text{bic}=k\ln(n)-2\ln\hat l$, where $n$ is the number of observations
- both reward a better fit (higher $\hat l$, so more negative $-2\ln\hat l$) while charging a cost per parameter — exactly occam's razor in one formula: a model that adds parameters must improve the fit by more than the added penalty to come out ahead
- because bic's penalty term $k\ln(n)$ grows with sample size while aic's stays fixed at $2k$, bic penalises extra parameters more heavily as $n$ grows and tends to favour simpler models than aic does on larger datasets
- only *differences* in aic/bic across candidate models are meaningful — the absolute value on its own says nothing
- aic and bic require a well-defined likelihood from a model fit by maximum likelihood (linear/logistic regression, other glms); they're cheap to compute once the model is fit, with no refitting or held-out data required, unlike [cross-validation](../training-evaluation/train-test.qmd#cross-validation), which works for any model and loss but costs $k$ refits
- for certain model classes, aic is asymptotically equivalent to leave-one-out cross-validation — a concrete bridge between this information-theoretic view of model complexity and the empirical, resampling-based view used elsewhere in these notes

## where it shows up

- [regularisation](../training-evaluation/regularisation.qmd) directly implements occam's razor: penalising large weights (or nonzero weights, for l1) is a concrete way of preferring the simplest model consistent with the data
- feature selection seeks the smallest sufficient set of features rather than using every available one — see [feature selection & extraction](../training-evaluation/feature-engineering.qmd#feature-selection--extraction)
- model selection: preferring a lower polynomial degree, a shallower tree, or fewer hidden units when accuracy is comparable across choices
- [baseline models](../training-evaluation/baseline-models.qmd) are the extreme version of this — always check whether a trivially simple model does almost as well before justifying something complex

## practical considerations

- occam's razor is a bias, not a law — it helps most when the true underlying relationship actually is simple, or close to it; forcing an overly simple model onto a genuinely complex relationship underfits, see [residuals & the bias–variance tradeoff](../training-evaluation/bias-variance.qmd)
- "simplest that fits" should be judged relative to how much data is available — a more complex model isn't wrong, just riskier without enough data to support it
- treat it as a heuristic to generate candidates, not a substitute for evaluation: use [cross-validation](../training-evaluation/train-test.qmd#cross-validation) or [learning curves](../training-evaluation/learning-curves.qmd) to check empirically whether the simpler model actually generalises better, rather than assuming it does
- reach for aic/bic when comparing nested or related glm-style models fit by maximum likelihood and refitting across folds is expensive; reach for cross-validation when comparing arbitrary models/pipelines, or when there's no clean likelihood to work with at all
